title: escalation-observability-and-retry-surge-controller
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary: During a customer escalation on 2025-02-11 we observed correlated 5xx spikes and timeouts originating from concentrated retry storms after a tenant migration. This ticket implements a deployable 'retry-surge-controller' plus expanded telemetry to prevent amplification and speed triage for future escalations.

Problem statement: Multiple customers reported intermittent 5xx responses and long tail timeouts. Root causes were multifactor: (1) clients re-sent requests after perceived timeouts while backend was temporarily saturated; (2) edge/frontdoor was re-issuing calls to the same downstream inference pool due to ambiguous retry semantics; (3) KV cache compaction during tenant re-shard caused transient latency spikes, which combined with client-side retries led to queue saturation and cascading 502/504s.

Goals:
- Stop short-lived retry amplification without requiring client changes.
- Provide clearer per-tenant telemetry for escalation owners (retry rate, dedup hits, per-tenant tail-latency heatmap).
- Introduce a safe server-side mitigation (retry-surge-controller) that gracefully sheds or delays retries while preserving best-effort throughput for high-priority tenants.

Proposed design:
1) Retry Surge Controller (RSC): a lightweight admission controller placed at the edge/router layer that fingerprints replays by (idempotency-token, request-path, tenant-id, recent-hash). When a burst of retries is detected (thresholds tunable by tenant and route), RSC will: 
   - return a fast 429 with Retry-After for low-priority retries, OR
   - queue and stagger retries with jitter for medium-priority, OR
   - allow through for priority customers (config-driven).
2) Server-side dedup window: a short-lived cache (per-edge instance) that collapses identical in-flight requests for up to 5s for known-idempotent routes. This reduces duplicate downstream execution.
3) Observability additions: new Grafana panels (per-tenant retry amplification ratio, in-flight dedup rate, kv-eviction correlation) plus a centralized retry-surge alert with automated incident links.
4) Rollout plan: Canary in hosted us-west for 48h with synthetic traffic that exercises retry storms, then progressive rollout by region and tenant risk group.

Trade-offs and notes:
- Dedup cache increases memory pressure and introduces a small correctness surface for non-idempotent routes; we will enable dedup only for explicit idempotent endpoints and require idempotency-token header for collapse.
- Returning 429 changes client behavior; we will add guidance in SDKs and set conservative default thresholds to avoid false positives.
- This is a stopgap mitigation; long-term work remains on KV compaction smoothing and edge connection pooling improvements.

Success criteria (SLOs):
- Reduce tenant-visible 5xx spike amplitude by >60% during synthetic retry storms.
- Reduce end-to-end request duplicates measured at the runtime layer by >70% for idempotent routes.
- Mean time to identify root cause for escalations of this type reduced from ~3h to <30m (thanks to telemetry).

Testing plan: unit + integration tests for dedup behavior, chaos experiment (controlled retry flood) in staging, canary run with CanaryGuard monitoring, and post-rollout verification queries against telemetry.
